q: Which state of matter has a definite shape and a definite volume?
e: Particles in a solid are locked in place, so it keeps both its shape and its volume.

q: A sealed balloon is squeezed into a smaller space and the gas inside takes up less volume. Why can the gas be compressed so easily?
o: its particles are heavier than a solid's
e: Gas particles have lots of empty space between them.

q: Water is poured from a tall glass into a wide bowl. What happens to its shape and volume?
o: shape changes, volume stays the same
shape stays the same, volume changes
e: A liquid takes the shape of its container but keeps its volume.

q: Compared with the particles in ice, the particles in water vapor have...
e: Gas particles move fastest, so they have the most kinetic energy.

q: Which statement describes the particles in a liquid?
o: they stay close together but slide past each other
they are fixed in rigid positions
they are far apart and move freely
they do not move at all
e: Liquid particles are close but can flow.

q: A solid is heated until it melts. What happens to the motion of its particles as the thermal energy increases?
o: they move slower and pack tighter
they move faster and break free of fixed positions
e: Added energy speeds particles up so they can slide past each other.

q: A student sees that a gas always fills its whole container, while a liquid does not. What explains the difference?
o: gas particles are larger than liquid particles
gas particles are attracted strongly to each other
gas particles spread out because they move freely with little attraction
e: Weak attractions let gas particles spread out to fill any space.

q: Which of these is a pure substance?
e: A pure substance has just one kind of matter; distilled water is only H2O.

q: Sugar is stirred into water until it can no longer be seen. This kind of mixture is called a...
e: A homogeneous mixture (solution) looks the same throughout.

q: A bowl of cereal with milk has separate pieces you can see. Which kind of matter is it?
e: The parts are not evenly mixed and can be seen.

q: Which is a homogeneous mixture?
e: Air looks uniform throughout, with gases evenly mixed.

q: Iron filings and sand are mixed together. Which method separates them using a physical property?
e: Iron is magnetic and sand is not.

q: Which is a way to separate saltwater into salt and water?
e: Heating drives off the water and leaves the salt behind.

q: Gold melts at a specific temperature, and the melted gold has the same properties as the solid. This suggests gold is a...
e: Pure substances have fixed, consistent properties.

q: Most elements on the periodic table are...
e: The majority of elements are metals.

q: A shiny element that is easily shaped and conducts electricity well is most likely a...
e: Luster, malleability and conductivity are metal properties.

q: An element is brittle when solid, dull, and a poor conductor of heat. It is most likely a...
e: Brittle, dull and poor conductivity describe nonmetals.

q: Silicon has properties between those of metals and nonmetals. It is classified as a...
e: Metalloids have mixed properties.

q: Silicon is used in computer chips because it can conduct electricity under some conditions but not others. This is a property of a...
e: Metalloids are semiconductors.

q: Rare Earth elements are important in modern life because they are used in...
o: magnets and electronics such as phones
e: Rare Earth elements are used in strong magnets, screens and batteries.

q: Copper is used for electrical wires because it is...
e: Copper is a metal that conducts electricity well.

q: A block of wood floats on water, but a rock of the same size sinks. Which has the greater density?
e: Objects denser than the fluid sink; less dense objects float.

q: An object has a mass of 20 g and a volume of 10 cm³. What is its density?
e: Density = mass ÷ volume = 20 ÷ 10.

q: Oil floats on top of water. What does this show?
o: oil has more mass in each cm³
oil is less dense than water
e: Less dense liquids float on denser ones.

q: A liquid has a density of 1.5 g/mL. A ball with a density of 1.2 g/mL is placed in it. What happens?
o: the ball stays at the bottom
e: The ball is less dense than the liquid.

q: A student has 50 g of lead and 50 g of foam. The foam takes up much more space. What does this show?
o: foam is less dense than lead
e: The same mass in a larger volume means lower density.

q: A steel ship floats even though steel is denser than water. Why?
o: the ship's overall shape holds air, lowering its average density
e: The ship's hollow shape makes its overall density less than water.

q: Three floating objects have densities of 0.2 g/cm³, 0.6 g/cm³ and 0.9 g/cm³. Which one floats highest in water?
o: all float at the same height
e: The least dense object floats highest.

q: Which is evidence of a chemical change?
o: bubbles of gas forming when two substances mix
e: A new gas forming is a sign of a new substance.

q: A match burns and gives off heat and light. What type of change is this?
e: Burning forms new substances and releases energy.

q: Mixing baking soda and vinegar makes fizzing bubbles. What does this show?
o: a new substance, a gas, was formed
e: Gas production is evidence of a chemical change.

q: A cut apple turns brown. This is most likely a...
e: A color change from reacting with oxygen forms a new substance.

q: Which is a physical change rather than a chemical change?
e: Chopping changes size, not the type of substance.

q: Two clear liquids are mixed and a solid forms in the cup. What is the solid called?
e: A solid formed from liquids in a chemical reaction is a precipitate.

q: A cold pack gets cold when its chemicals are mixed. Which evidence of chemical change is this?
o: a change in volume of the pack
e: Absorbing or releasing heat can show a chemical change.

q: What force pulls objects toward Earth?
e: Gravity is the force of attraction toward Earth's center.

q: A book slides across a table and slows to a stop. Which force slows it down?
e: Friction opposes motion between surfaces.

q: A book rests on a table. Which force from the table pushes up on the book?
e: The normal force is perpendicular to the surface and supports the object.

q: A student pushes a shopping cart across the floor. The push is an example of a(n)...
e: An applied force comes from a person or object acting on something.

q: A refrigerator magnet sticks to a metal door. Which force holds it there?
e: Magnetic attraction pulls the magnet to the iron door.

q: Why does a skater glide farther on smooth ice than on a rough sidewalk?
o: there is less friction on ice
there is more gravity on ice
the skater is lighter on ice
e: Smoother surfaces create less friction.

q: Which action increases friction between a bike tire and the road?
o: letting the tires wear completely smooth
e: Rough surfaces increase friction.

q: Two students push on a box in opposite directions, each with 20 N. What is the net force?
e: Equal opposite forces cancel, so the forces are balanced.

q: A box is pushed right with 30 N and left with 10 N. What is the net force?
e: 30 − 10 = 20, in the direction of the bigger force.

q: When forces on an object are balanced, the object...
o: stays at rest or keeps moving at constant velocity
e: Balanced forces do not change motion.

q: A rope is pulled left with 50 N and right with 35 N. What is the net force and what will happen?
o: 15 N right; the rope accelerates right
15 N left; the rope accelerates left
85 N left; the rope stays still
e: Unbalanced forces cause acceleration toward the bigger force.

q: A book on a table has a 10 N weight pulling down and the table pushes up with 10 N. The forces are...
e: Equal and opposite forces are balanced, so the book stays at rest.

q: A cart is pushed forward with 25 N and friction pushes back with 5 N. What is the net force?
e: 25 − 5 = 20 in the forward direction.

q: Which diagram shows unbalanced forces? An arrow of 8 N right and an arrow of 3 N left. The net force is...
e: 8 − 3 = 5 toward the larger force.

q: According to Newton's Third Law, forces always come in...
e: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

q: A swimmer pushes backward on the water. What pushes the swimmer forward?
o: the water pushes back on the swimmer
e: The reaction force from the water is equal and opposite.

q: When a rocket expels gas downward, the rocket moves upward. This is an example of...
e: The gas is pushed down, so the rocket is pushed up.

q: A person pushes on a wall with 30 N of force. How much force does the wall push back with?
e: Action and reaction forces are equal in size.

q: A bat hits a ball. The bat exerts a force on the ball. What also happens?
o: the ball exerts a larger force
the ball exerts an equal and opposite force on the bat
e: Force pairs act on different objects.

q: A person jumps off a small boat and the boat moves backward. Why?
o: the water pushes the boat only
the boat is lighter than the water
the person pushes the boat backward as the boat pushes the person forward
e: The two objects push on each other with equal and opposite forces.

q: Why do the action and reaction forces not cancel each other?
o: one of them is not a real force
they act in the same direction
e: Cancelling needs forces on the same object.

q: A ball held high above the ground has which type of energy?
e: Height gives an object stored energy due to gravity.

q: A stretched rubber band has which type of energy?
e: Stretching stores energy in the band.

q: The energy stored in food and fuel is called...
e: Chemical bonds store energy.

q: A moving skateboard has...
e: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion.

q: A roller coaster car is at the top of a hill. As it rolls down, its potential energy...
o: decreases while its kinetic energy increases
increases while its kinetic energy decreases
e: Stored energy changes into motion as it falls.

q: Which has the most kinetic energy: a 2 kg ball moving at 5 m/s or a 2 kg ball moving at 10 m/s?
e: Faster objects have more kinetic energy.

q: A compressed spring is released and a toy shoots forward. Which energy change occurred?
e: Stored spring energy became motion.

q: The law of conservation of energy says that energy...
o: cannot be created or destroyed, only transformed
e: Total energy stays constant.

q: In photosynthesis, plants transform light energy into...
e: Plants store the energy in sugar molecules.

q: In an electrical circuit with a light bulb, electrical energy is transformed mostly into...
e: The bulb glows and gets warm.

q: In a food web, a rabbit eats grass and a fox eats the rabbit. Energy from the Sun ends up where?
o: gone after the grass is eaten
stored in the grass, then passed to the rabbit and fox
e: Energy flows through the web by eating.

q: A roller coaster never reaches a hill as high as the first one. Where does some of the energy go?
o: it is created again at the top
it is transformed into thermal energy by friction
e: Friction changes some mechanical energy into heat.

q: A battery-powered toy car moves. Which energy transformation occurs?
e: The battery's chemical energy powers a motor.

q: A pendulum swings back and forth and eventually stops. Why?
o: its mechanical energy is gradually transferred to thermal energy by air resistance and friction
e: No energy is lost; it is transferred to the surroundings.

q: In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium move...
o: in the same direction as the wave
at right angles to the direction the wave travels
e: Like a rope wave moving up and down while traveling across.

q: In a longitudinal wave, the particles move...
o: at right angles to the wave
back and forth parallel to the direction the wave travels
e: Compressions and expansions travel along the same line.

q: Sound waves are an example of which kind of wave?
e: Sound is made of compressions and rarefactions.

q: Waves transfer...
o: energy without moving matter along with them
e: A wave carries energy; the medium only vibrates.

q: A water wave moves a floating cork. What does the cork mainly do?
o: travel with the wave to shore
bob up and down in place
e: The medium moves in place while energy moves on.

q: The highest point of a transverse wave is called the...
e: The crest is the top of the wave.

q: The distance between two crests of a transverse wave is the...
e: Wavelength is the crest-to-crest distance.

q: What causes the seasons on Earth?
o: Earth's distance from the Sun changing a lot
the tilt of Earth's axis as it revolves around the Sun
the Sun getting bigger and smaller
e: Tilt changes how directly sunlight hits each hemisphere.

q: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it is...
e: Direct sunlight and longer days bring summer.

q: It is winter in Texas. What season is it in Australia?
e: Hemispheres have opposite seasons.

q: About how long does it take Earth to revolve once around the Sun?
e: A revolution takes about 365 days.

q: If Earth's axis were not tilted, what would happen to the seasons?
o: there would be little or no seasonal change
e: Tilt causes seasons.

q: On the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere, the Sun's rays are...
o: least direct and the day is shortest
most direct and the day is longest
e: The Northern Hemisphere is tilted most toward the Sun.

q: Why is it not hotter in the whole world when Earth is closest to the Sun in January?
o: seasons are caused by tilt, not distance
e: Earth's tilt, not distance, drives seasons.

q: What mainly causes ocean tides?
o: the gravity of the Moon and Sun
e: Gravitational pull from the Moon and Sun creates tides.

q: How many high tides do most coasts have each day?
e: Most places have two high and two low tides a day.

q: Spring tides (very high and very low) occur when the Sun, Earth and Moon are...
o: on opposite sides of the galaxy
e: The combined pull is strongest at new and full moon.

q: Neap tides (small tidal range) occur when the Sun and Moon are...
e: Their pulls partly cancel at first and third quarter moon.

q: At which Moon phase do spring tides occur?
e: The Sun, Earth and Moon line up at new and full moon.

q: At which Moon phase do neap tides occur?
e: The pulls act at right angles.

q: Why does the tide go in and out about twice a day at a beach?
o: Earth rotates under the tidal bulges
the Moon moves around the beach
e: Earth's rotation moves coasts through the bulges.

q: Which Earth system includes all living things?
e: The biosphere is all life on Earth.

q: Which Earth system includes oceans, lakes and rivers?
e: Hydro means water.

q: Which Earth system is the layer of gases surrounding the planet?
e: The atmosphere is made of air.

q: Rocks, soil and mountains belong to which Earth system?
e: The geosphere is the solid Earth.

q: A volcano erupts and sends ash into the air. Which two systems interact?
e: Rock material from the geosphere enters the air.

q: A tree absorbs water from soil and releases oxygen. Which systems are involved?
e: All four interact.

q: Which is part of the hydrosphere?
e: Frozen water is part of the hydrosphere.

q: Which layer of Earth is the thin, outermost layer?
e: The crust is the thin outer shell.

q: Which layer of Earth is the thickest?
e: The mantle makes up most of Earth's volume.

q: Which layer of Earth is made of solid iron and nickel because of the huge pressure?
e: Pressure keeps the inner core solid despite the heat.

q: Which layer of Earth is liquid metal?
e: The outer core is molten iron and nickel.

q: From the surface moving toward the center, which order of layers is correct?
o: mantle, crust, inner core, outer core
crust, outer core, mantle, inner core
crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
inner core, outer core, mantle, crust
e: Layers get hotter and deeper going inward.

q: Which layer's slow flowing movement helps move Earth's tectonic plates?
e: Convection in the mantle drives plate movement.

q: Earth's layers are sometimes modeled with a peach. What does the pit most likely represent?
e: The pit is the center, like the core.

q: Rock formed from cooled magma or lava is called...
e: Igneous means formed from fire/melt.

q: Rock formed from layers of pressed sediment is called...
e: Layers of sediment get compacted and cemented.

q: Rock changed by heat and pressure without melting is called...
e: Metamorphic means changed in form.

q: Which rock is most likely to contain fossils?
o: metamorphic rock made at great depth
e: Fossils are preserved in sediment layers.

q: Limestone is heated and squeezed deep underground and becomes marble. Marble is a...
e: Heat and pressure changed it.

q: Which process turns rock into small pieces that can become sediment?
e: Rocks break down and are moved.

q: Granite cools slowly from magma. Over time it is weathered into sand. The sand is then pressed into sandstone. Which sequence of rock types is correct?
o: igneous, then metamorphic with no steps
e: Weathering and compaction produce sedimentary rock.

q: Why is managing natural resources important?
o: so people and ecosystems can keep having enough clean water, food and energy
so resources are used up faster
e: Careful use makes resources last.

q: Burning fossil fuels for energy can cause what environmental problem?
e: Burning fuels releases pollutants.

q: Poor management of water resources can lead to...
e: Overuse and contamination hurt supplies.

q: How can reducing energy waste help with global poverty?
o: lower energy costs leave more money for food, health care and education
e: Savings can be used for basic needs.

q: Which is an effect of malnutrition that better food resource management may reduce?
e: Managing food supplies helps people get enough nutrients.

q: Which resource problem is caused by polluted air?
e: Air pollution harms lungs.

q: A city wastes much of its drinking water through leaky pipes. Which result is most likely?
o: less water available for people and higher costs
e: Wasted water reduces supply and raises costs.

q: Which action conserves energy at home?
o: leaving the TV on all day
turning off lights when leaving a room
e: Using less energy conserves it.

q: Which is a way to conserve water?
e: Using less water saves it.

q: An LED light bulb uses much less electricity than an older bulb to produce the same light. This is an example of...
e: Efficiency means getting the same result using less energy.

q: Planting cover crops helps protect which resource?
e: Roots and plants hold soil and reduce erosion.

q: A power plant adds scrubbers that remove pollutants from smoke before it is released. This technology helps manage...
e: Scrubbers clean exhaust gases.

q: Which technology helps manage energy resources by making use of the Sun?
e: Solar panels convert sunlight to electricity.

q: Recycling aluminum cans saves energy because...
o: making new cans from recycled metal takes far less energy than from raw ore
e: Recycling avoids energy-heavy mining and refining.

q: Two plants in the same patch compete for water and light. What happens if there is not enough of one resource?
o: some plants grow poorly or die
e: Limited resources limit population size.

q: If a drought reduces water in a pond ecosystem, what will most likely happen to fish populations?
o: they will stay exactly the same
e: Less water means less habitat and food.

q: Rabbits in a field eat the available grass. What happens to the rabbit population if the grass supply drops sharply?
e: Less food reduces how many rabbits can survive.

q: A new species of fish is added to a lake and eats the same food as native fish. What is likely to occur?
e: Sharing a limited resource creates competition.

q: Which change in an abiotic factor would most harm a coral reef ecosystem?
o: more algae in a healthy balance
more sunlight in the right range
e: Coral is sensitive to temperature.

q: In a desert ecosystem, cactuses, snakes and sand are all present. Which of these is an abiotic part of the ecosystem?
e: Sand is non-living; cactuses and animals are living.

q: Coyotes and foxes in the same area both hunt rabbits. When rabbits become scarce, what is the most likely effect on the two predator populations?
o: both populations face competition and may decline
e: Fewer shared prey means more competition for food.

q: An owl hunts and eats mice. The owl is the...
e: Predators hunt and eat prey.

q: A tick feeds on a dog's blood and harms the dog. This is...
e: One organism benefits, the other is harmed.

q: Bees collect nectar from flowers and pollinate them. This is...
e: Both organisms benefit.

q: A barnacle attaches to a whale. The barnacle gets a ride and food, and the whale is not affected. This is...
e: One benefits and the other is neither helped nor harmed.

q: Two male deer fight for territory. This is an example of...
e: Organisms compete for limited resources.

q: A clownfish lives among a sea anemone's stinging tentacles, gaining protection, while it cleans the anemone and drives away fish that eat it. This is...
e: Both species gain.

q: A mistletoe plant grows on a tree, taking water and nutrients from it and weakening it. The mistletoe is a...
e: It benefits at the tree's expense.

q: A single living thing is called a(n)...
e: Organism is the smallest level of ecological organization.

q: All the deer living in one forest make up a...
e: A population is one species in one area.

q: All the populations of different species living together in an area make up a...
e: A community includes all species there.

q: A community plus the non-living factors such as water, soil and sunlight is a(n)...
e: An ecosystem includes biotic and abiotic parts.

q: Which list is in order from smallest to largest?
e: Each level contains the one before it.

q: A scientist counts all the frogs in a pond. What level of organization is she studying?
e: Frogs of one species form a population.

q: A scientist studies the frogs, fish, plants and insects in a pond. She is studying a...
e: Several species living together form a community.

q: What is the basic unit of structure and function in living things?
e: Cells are the building blocks of life.

q: According to cell theory, new cells come from...
e: Cells divide to form new cells.

q: According to cell theory, all living things are made of...
e: Even single-celled organisms are made of a cell.

q: Which scientist is credited with first observing and naming cells in cork?
e: Hooke used a microscope in the 1600s.

q: Why was the invention of the microscope important for cell theory?
o: it removed the need for experiments
it allowed scientists to see cells
e: Cells are too small to see without magnification.

q: A student sees a single cell that moves, eats and reproduces. What does this suggest about it?
o: it is a complete living organism
it is just a part of a bigger animal
e: A single cell can carry out all life processes.

q: Which statement is part of cell theory?
o: cells are not found in plants
cells are the basic unit of life
cells can come from nonliving things
cells are made by the nucleus only
e: That is one of the three main ideas.

q: A cell without a nucleus, such as a bacterium, is called...
e: Prokaryotes lack a nucleus.

q: Plant and animal cells have a nucleus. They are classified as...
e: Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.

q: A paramecium is made of a single cell. It is...
e: Unicellular means one cell.

q: An organism that makes its own food from sunlight is called...
e: Autotrophs produce their own food.

q: An organism that must eat other organisms for food is called...
e: Heterotrophs consume other organisms.

q: A tree is a multicellular, eukaryotic autotroph. Which organism has the same set of characteristics?
e: A sunflower is a plant, so it is multicellular, eukaryotic and photosynthetic.

q: A mushroom has a nucleus, many cells, and absorbs food from decaying matter. It is...
e: Fungi are heterotrophic eukaryotes.

q: Why are differences among organisms in a population important?
o: some may survive better when the environment changes
e: Variation gives a chance that some will survive.

q: A beetle population has green and brown individuals. Birds see the green ones more easily against brown bark. Which are more likely to survive and reproduce?
e: Camouflaged individuals avoid predators.

q: A drought makes plants with deeper roots more likely to survive. This is an example of...
o: a change that cannot be inherited
e: Deep roots reach water.

q: A disease kills most individuals in a population, but a few with a resistant trait survive. What is likely true of the next generation?
o: more will have the resistant trait
e: Survivors pass the trait on.

q: Why can a population with little variation be at risk when a disease appears?
o: it gains new traits at once
if all are vulnerable, all could die
e: Without variation, there may be no resistant individuals.

q: As an environment gets colder, which trait would be an advantage for a mammal?
e: Insulation helps in the cold.

q: A trait that helps an organism survive in one environment may be a disadvantage in another. Which example fits this?
o: green leaves help only in snow
white fur helps in snow but stands out in a forest
e: A trait's value depends on the environment.
